newsitem.title: CANADA: Thomson says ahead on debt-cutting plans.
newsitem.headline: Thomson says ahead on debt-cutting plans.

text.p: Thomson Corp president and chief executive Michael Brown said the company has made more headway than expected in tackling the debt load it acquired with its US$3.4 billion takeover of West Publishing Co.

"At the time of the West deal, we predicted a debt-equity ratio of 1.3 to 1.0 by the end of this year. We always said that insofar as possible, we try to keep it at 1.0 to 1.0," Brown told Reuters in an interview.
"Since then we have made a couple of further divestments, nothing of any scale. And we have been doing well in generating cash flow," he added.

Brown said that by year end, Thomson's debt-to-equity ratio -- closely watched by financial analysts and debt-rating agencies -- would be slightly above 1.1 to 1.0, below the forecast made at the time of the West deal.

Brown said Thomson did not give earnings forecasts, but added that he was "not uncomfortable" with analysts' consensus estimates for 1996. The mean estimate for the year is about US$0.84 a share, including a US$0.05 per share dilution from the recently completed West deal.

Brown said Thomson's travel group should have a good year in 1996, pumping out 200 million pounds sterling of cash in 1996 and 125 million pounds sterling in 1997 (1 STG = US$1.56). Analysts have clamored for Thomson to sell its travel holdings, but Brown said that was not in the cards at the moment.
But in the longer run the group may not constitute a logical piece of the Thomson puzzle -- increasingly dominated by specialty and professional publishing.

"While travel isn't for sale, we have had offers. We have rejected them all. And the fact is, the business today is worth massively more than it was 10 years ago...so we were right to keep it," Brown said.

"You look at the logic and see that right out in the dim distant future, the business will come apart. But short term I have got to say...we have no intention right now of selling that business," he added.
Brown said the US$1 billion price tag some analysts had put on the group was inadequate, although he stated that it was a moot point since the division was not on the block.
"I think a business that makes 200 million pounds cash flow is worth a lot more than US$1 billion," Brown said.
Travel, which includes Britannia Airways and the British Lunn Poly chain of travel agencies, was rumored as a likely divestment because of Thomson's recent heavy emphasis on specialty publishing.
The acquisition of West is a cornerstone of the new Thomson -- one which garners just 13 percent of its revenue from advertising, far lower than a decade ago.
Brown said there was no merit to last week's legal filing opposing the West purchase by the Lexis-Nexis division of Anglo-Dutch publishing and information group Reed Elsevier.
"The words I have read from them seem to indicate that they have made a really bad job of buying Lexis-Nexis...They're showing desparation," he said.
The West deal has been approved by the U.S. Justice Department, which asked Thomson to shed 70 products the department valued at about US$275 million.

"They had a very, very comprehensive list of what we should divest and we are in the process of doing just that. We are working with a number of buyers," said Brown. He said the US$250 million figure was determined by the Justice Department and not based on Thomson forecasts.
After a rapid run of acquisitions -- Brown said Thomson was averaging one a week in 1995 -- Thomson would likely slow down and focus on "organic growth" in the near term.
"We are not proactively seeking a major strategic acquisition at the moment. But if something comes up unsolicited, we've got to look at it and respond," Brown said.
"I think where we would most like to see acquisitions...where we see the perhaps the greatest change and fastest growth are in financial services and healthcare," he added.
The divestiture of a substantial part of the newspaper group was largely complete, although a few more papers may go on the block before the end of the year, Brown said.
-- Reuters Toronto Bureau 416-941-8100
